shorts.title: Haley Stevens, Asked About El-Sayed: "I'm On The Team" #Shorts
shorts.hook: A Democrat Won't Say Her Nominee's Name
shorts.narration: [deadpan] Michigan Democrats, one week before the election. Congresswoman Haley Stevens lost the Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed. Sunday on CNN, she was asked about him. [beat] [amused] She never said his name. She said, quote, "if you had asked me if I'm still on the team, I'm on the team." Folks, that's not an endorsement. That's a hostage video. [beat] [sarcastic] She added, "I can't say that I agree with everything that's gone on." Then Indivisible's Leah Greenberg told Democrats who won't fully endorse to get off television. Matthew twelve, twenty-five: "Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation." [beat] [emphatic] Blue no matter who? More like blue, no matter what we say on TV. Democrats, is this a team, or a group chat nobody wants to leave? Tell me below. Subscribe, friends. Henry roasts the news every day.

claims.text: Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic Senate primary in Michigan to Abdul El-Sayed, said on CNN's State of the Union: "Well, look, I would just say, if you had asked me if I'm still on the team, I'm on the team." Asked about El-Sayed, she did not name him.
Stevens also said: "I can't say that I agree with everything that's gone on."

Indivisible's Leah Greenberg wrote that Democrats who cannot give a full-throated endorsement to the Democratic nominee should "stay the f--- off television." The article says the midterms were about a week away.

claims.text: The New York Times reported on October 20 that Trump had discussed replacing the briefing room with an indoor swimming pool; Trump denied it on Truth Social on Saturday and Sunday.

Trump wrote on Truth Social Sunday: "I am not building a swimming pool in the White House Briefing Room, and never had any intention of doing so" and "I am thinking about moving the Press, and putting them in a different location."
The White House indoor pool opened in 1933 for FDR, and President Nixon later had a briefing room built above the old pool.

claims.text: Alaska's Senate ballot includes two candidates named Dan Sullivan: Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan and Daniel J. Sullivan, who will have no party affiliation; Republicans tried for months to remove him and lost at the Alaska Supreme Court.
Trump said Friday he directed the Justice Department to sue; the suit seeks to block certification if the incumbent loses. Trump said: "I'm the one who said do it."
Election experts said such lawsuits are rare and that the case relies on a novel reading of the National Voter Registration Act.

shorts.title: Judge Furman To Trump DOJ: "Flies In The Face" Of Two Centuries #Shorts
shorts.hook: A Judge Rejects DOJ's Article II Claim
shorts.narration: [serious] A Manhattan federal judge, Jesse Furman, just ruled against the Trump Justice Department. He found the firing of prosecutor Maurene Comey unlawful and ordered her reinstated with back pay. [beat] [deadpan] The DOJ conceded it wasn't for cause or performance. Its argument was Article II. The judge said that, quote, "flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent." [beat] [sarcastic] Two centuries. That's a lot of homework to skip. The DOJ says it disagrees and will appeal, quote, "in due course." Proverbs eighteen, seventeen: "He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him." [beat] [emphatic] Round one goes to the judge. Round two goes to the appeals court. Conservatives, does the president really have unlimited firing power? Tell me in the comments. claims.text: Judge Jesse Furman, nominated by Obama, ruled the Justice Department's firing of Maurene Comey unlawful and ordered her reinstated with back pay through December 20, 2025.
The DOJ acknowledged the firing was not for cause and not based on performance but argued Article II gave the attorney general authority to remove her.
Furman wrote the argument "flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent"; a DOJ spokesperson said the department disagreed and would appeal "in due course."
